subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

edits.note: 'if a new student joined your school and could not read the signs' is the whole thought experiment; the day is not part of it

periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students share their own bus travel experiences and describe what they saw on the way (p. 35)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Rishi's bus journey through hairpin roads

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening of the chapter — Rishi boarding a bus, the hairpin roads, the flower-covered hills — pausing to let children picture the scene. Ask: What do you imagine you would see from a bus window on a winding mountain road?

Students open Textbook p. 35 and discuss in pairs: Have you ever travelled by bus? What did you see — roads, trees, buildings, fields? Pairs share with the class, building a collective picture of journeys children have taken.

Whole-class discussion moves to what different children noticed about trees, flowers, and landscapes on their journeys. The teacher lists flower and tree names on the board as children name them, comparing familiar local sightings with what Rishi saw in the Himalayas.

Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks about one journey they remember — where they went, how they travelled, and one thing in nature they noticed along the way. The teacher circulates and prompts those who have not travelled far to describe their neighbourhood surroundings.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe a journey using observations of the natural environment seen along the way.
periods.section_context: Bus travel experience, hairpin mountain roads, flower-covered hills, Rishi's journey to the Himalayan village
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Did anyone notice the same flower or tree in two different places on their journey — what was different about how it looked? Prompt children who have not travelled by bus to recall a walk, auto-ride, or cycle trip instead.

periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students draw and label three road signboards not listed in the textbook (p. 36)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 36 and complete the match-the-column activity pairing road signboards with their meanings. The teacher briefly discusses each match as a class to confirm understanding of what each sign tells a traveller or driver.

Students recall road signs they have seen on their way to school or during travel — stop signs, school-zone signs, no-entry signs, speed-limit boards, pedestrian crossings. The teacher lists suggestions on the board and the class discusses what each sign protects people from.

Each student draws and labels three road signboards they have seen but that are not in the textbook list. Drawings include the sign's shape, symbol or text, and a short label explaining its meaning. Encourage children to invent clear, readable symbols.

A quick gallery moment: students hold up their drawings and two or three children explain one sign each to the class. The teacher highlights that road signs keep everyone — walkers, cyclists, and drivers — safe.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent safety information visually through labelled diagrams or signs.
periods.section_context: Road signboard match activity, drawing and labelling three unlisted road signs, travel safety
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Why do you think the sign uses a picture rather than just words? Prompt children to think about who needs to read signs quickly and why symbols work across languages.

periods.activity_title: Safe Journeys: Travel and Road Safety Rules
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students discuss safety measures to take while travelling and while riding a bicycle and walking on the road (p. 35)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to recall Rishi's bus journey on steep hairpin roads and asks: What might have made that journey risky? Students offer ideas — sharp bends, narrow roads, height — and the teacher connects these to why safe behaviour on roads and in vehicles matters.

Students open Textbook p. 35 and discuss in small groups: What safety measures should you take while travelling in a bus or car? Groups share rules — sitting still, not leaning out of windows, wearing seat belts, listening to the driver. The teacher lists agreed rules on the board.

Discussion shifts to cycling and walking: What should you do when riding a bicycle? What about walking on a busy road? Students share their own practices and experiences. The teacher adds any important rules not yet mentioned — using footpaths, looking both ways, wearing a helmet.

Each student writes a personal 'My Safe Travel Rules' list of at least four rules in their notebook — at least two for vehicles and two for cycling or walking. The teacher invites two or three students to read their lists aloud and the class affirms or adds to each.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate and apply safety rules for different modes of travel and road use.
periods.section_context: Safety measures during bus or vehicle travel, safety while riding a bicycle, safety while walking on the road, hairpin mountain roads
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Has anyone ever seen someone get hurt because they did not follow a road rule — what happened? Encourage children to practise one rule they will try on their way home today, and keep the tone constructive rather than frightening.

periods.activity_title: Flowers of Spring: Recognising Regional Blooms
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students find out about mountains, rivers, or streams near where they live and about visiting relatives in far-away places (p. 42)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of tulip, buransh/Rhododendron, amaltas, sakhua flowers

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the section aloud where Rishi sees the garden full of flowers — rose, marigold, hibiscus, and then the unfamiliar tulip and buransh. Students point to the textbook illustrations as each flower is named. Ask: Which flowers do you already know? Which are new to you?

Students observe the textbook illustrations carefully and record in their notebooks a simple two-column table: Flower Name | Where it grows / Which region. They fill in details from the text for tulip (Kashmir), buransh/Rhododendron (Jammu), amaltas (Kerala), and sakhua (Jharkhand), then add any local flower they know from their own region.

Class discussion: Why do different flowers bloom in different places? The teacher draws out ideas about climate, altitude, and season — using the 'Do You Know' box about the Himalayas meaning 'home of snow' and Mount Everest's height to show how dramatically environments differ. Children connect cooler highland air to different plant life.

Each student draws one flower from the chapter they found most interesting, labels it with its name and home region, and writes one sentence about what makes it special. A few students share their drawings with the class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record diversity among plants by matching them to the regional environments in which they grow.
periods.section_context: Rose, marigold, hibiscus, tulip (Kashmir), buransh/Rhododendron (Jammu), amaltas (Kerala), sakhua (Jharkhand), Himalayan altitude and climate, Do You Know box on Himalayas and Mount Everest
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Have you ever seen a flower growing wild near your home or on a hillside — do you know its name in your language? Prompt children to consider how altitude and cold might stop some flowers from growing in certain places.

periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students sing the spring song together (p. 40)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations or descriptions of Tulip Festival, Vishu Kani, Sarhul

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 40 and sing the spring song together — 'Oh! Spring is in the air…' The teacher leads two rounds, encouraging clapping or swaying. Ask: What images does the song make you picture? What season is arriving in the song?

The teacher leads a shared reading of the festival descriptions: Kashmir Tulip Festival, Rishi's Jammu spring ritual with mustard and buransh flowers at doorsteps and elders giving blessings and sweets, Kerala's Vishu with amaltas flowers and the Vishu Kani ritual, and the Sarhul festival from the 'Do You Know' box — the procession to the sakhua tree, offerings to Earth and Sun, dhol and nagada. Students listen and discuss: What do all these festivals have in common?

Small-group discussion: each group is given one festival to talk about — what flower, what ritual, what food or offering, what feeling it creates. Groups report back and the teacher notes commonalities on the board: flowers + seasonal change + community gathering + joy. Mami's explanation — 'Spring is a celebration of nature' — is written on the board as a shared idea.

Each student writes two or three sentences in their notebook about one spring festival they found most interesting — what happens, which flower is part of it, and why they think people celebrate it. Children who know a spring festival from their own community are encouraged to write about that instead.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a seasonal change in nature and the cultural practices communities develop in response to it.
periods.section_context: Kashmir Tulip Festival, Jammu spring ritual with mustard and buransh flowers and elders' blessings, Kerala Vishu with amaltas and Vishu Kani, Sarhul in Jharkhand with sakhua flowers and offerings to Earth and Sun, dhol and nagada, spring song
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: In your family or community, is there something special you do when a particular flower blooms or when a new season begins — what is it called? The Sarhul description is a rich opportunity to draw out how trees and nature are honoured in traditional practices; invite children to share similar customs without naming the tradition by its origin.

periods.activity_title: Festival Foods and Clothes: An Inquiry with Elders
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students ask elders about festivals celebrated in their locality for each season and list special foods prepared during them (p. 40)

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the inquiry task from Textbook p. 40: finding out which festivals happen in each season in students' own locality and what special food is made. Students discuss briefly: Who at home would know the most about festival foods and when festivals happen? The class agrees that asking elders is the most reliable source.

Students set up the season table in their notebooks — four rows for the four seasons — and begin filling in what they already know from home experience: festival names, foods eaten, and the season. The teacher circulates, helping children name seasons correctly and spelling festival and food names.

Students open Textbook p. 41 and complete the food-festival matching activity: Thekua–Chhath Puja, Pitha–Bihu, Plum Cake–Christmas, Gujiya–Holi, Sadya–Onam, Holige–Ugadi, Seviyan–Eid-ul-Fitr. The teacher discusses which festivals children already knew and which are new to them, noting the geographical spread.

Students write a short response to the question on Textbook p. 41: What special dresses do you wear during festivals? They also write one question they want to ask an elder at home to add more festivals to their season table. The teacher notes: everyone's list will look different, and that diversity is exactly the point.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple structured inquiry by drawing on elder knowledge to document seasonal festivals, foods, and clothing practices in their own community.
periods.section_context: Season-wise festival and food inquiry table, festival food matching: Thekua-Chhath Puja, Pitha-Bihu, Plum Cake-Christmas, Gujiya-Holi, Sadya-Onam, Holige-Ugadi, Seviyan-Eid-ul-Fitr, festival dress, haakh with rice (Kashmiri meal)
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Are there any foods your family only makes during one particular festival — what would happen if you tried to eat it on a normal day? Prompt children to consider whether the same festival food might be made differently in different families or regions, and celebrate that variation rather than looking for a single correct answer.

periods.activity_title: Let Us Reflect: Discussion and Writing
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss how festivals and celebrations bring communities together (p. 42)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 42 and the class works through the five discussion prompts together: modes of transport during travel; staying safe on journeys; special foods at festivals; how festivals bring communities together; and feeling happy in nature. The teacher takes each prompt in turn, inviting several children to respond before moving on.

Focused discussion on the fourth prompt — how festivals bring people together. Students share examples: relatives arriving from far away, everyone wearing new clothes, cooking together, singing and dancing. The teacher connects this to the chapter: Rishi travelling to his Mama's house, all the cousins playing, the exchange of festival knowledge across regions.

Students write their two reflection responses from Textbook p. 42: naming two relatives they have visited recently, and describing how they spend time with cousins and relatives. The teacher encourages specific, concrete details — games played, food eaten, stories told — rather than general statements.

Students complete the fill-in-the-blanks exercise from Textbook p. 42, using knowledge from the chapter: mountains, hairpin roads, mud road, buransh, haakh. The teacher reads each blank aloud and the class checks answers together at the end.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect personal experiences of family and community gatherings to the broader idea that festivals and celebrations build bonds across distances.
periods.section_context: Five discuss prompts on transport, travel safety, festival foods, festivals bringing communities together, joy in nature; write tasks about relatives visited and time with cousins; fill-in-the-blanks: mountains, hairpin roads, mud road, buransh, haakh
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Has a festival ever brought someone to your home who you had not seen for a long time — how did that feel? Where responses to the fill-in-the-blanks differ from the textbook (regional names), affirm them before offering the textbook answer.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students design signboards for school spaces on chart paper and explain their creations (p. 43)
materials: Chart paper (one sheet per student or pair)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 43 showing the list of school spaces to be signed

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 43 and read the task together: designing signboards for school library, toilet, assembly area, drinking water point, playground, classroom, and stairs. The teacher recalls the road signboard discussion from the earlier unit on travel safety — ask: What made those signs easy to understand quickly?

Quick planning moment: students decide which two or three school spaces they will design signs for, choosing their symbols and colours. The teacher reminds them that a good sign is clear to someone who cannot read — it uses pictures, shapes, and colour as the main message.

Students work on their chart-paper signboards — drawing, colouring, and labelling each sign with the space's name and a short explanation of what the symbol means. The teacher circulates, asking children to explain their choices: Why did you choose that shape? Why that colour?

Each student or pair holds up their signboards and gives a brief explanation of what they created and why. The class offers one positive observation for each. The teacher closes by connecting the activity back to Rishi's journey: road signs kept him safe travelling to the mountains; school signs help everyone move through a shared space with care.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and explain visual signs that communicate purpose or direction clearly to a shared community of users.
periods.section_context: School signboard design task for library, toilet, assembly area, drinking water point, playground, classroom, stairs; symbol and colour choices; explaining created signs
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: If a new student joined your school and could not read the signs, which of your signs would still help them — why? Encourage children who share a home language to think about whether their symbol would work for someone from a different region.

assessment_items.question_text: Rishi travelled from Jammu to visit his cousins in a mountain village. On the way, the bus went along hairpin roads with hills covered in flowers. Which of the following best describes what Rishi was most likely observing during his journey?

options.label: A
options.text: The clothes worn by other passengers on the bus

options.label: B
options.text: The flowers, trees, and landscape along the mountain road

options.label: C
options.text: The kinds of food being sold at roadside shops

options.label: D
options.text: The names of the villages the bus passed through

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests whether students understand that observing the natural environment — flowers, trees, landscape — is the key activity of Rishi's journey, as described in the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe a journey using observations of the natural environment seen along the way.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing a social/commercial detail with the natural observation focus of the chapter — they have not connected the journey narrative to nature observation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has recalled a journey detail (place names, route) rather than the nature-observation emphasis of the section, suggesting surface reading of the text.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has focused on a human/social feature of travel rather than the environmental observation that drives Rishi's experience in this chapter.

assessment_items.task: Draw two road signs — one that tells drivers to be careful, and one that helps a pedestrian or cyclist stay safe. Label each sign with its name and write one sentence explaining what it means.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about signs you have seen near your school, on busy roads, or in the chapter. Draw the sign shape first, then add the symbol or words. Write the sign's name below it and one sentence: 'This sign means ___.'
format_of_output: Two labelled drawings of road signs
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any road signs the student has observed — stop signs, school-zone warnings, pedestrian crossings, no-entry signs, speed limits, cycle-lane markers. Signs need not match the textbook list exactly; assess whether the symbol communicates a safety meaning and whether the label and sentence are consistent with the drawing.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent safety information visually through labelled diagrams or signs.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate a safety idea into a visual symbol and explain its meaning — showing they understand that signs encode information for quick reading by a community of users.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks students through the making sequence: shape → symbol → label → sentence. A student who skips the sentence has not fully demonstrated the communicative purpose of the sign.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: clearly recognisable symbol, accurate label, and a sentence that correctly explains the sign's protective purpose. Weak: a drawing without a label or with a sentence that contradicts the symbol, or a decorative image with no safety meaning.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who have not seen many road signs may draw a sign for a pedestrian crossing near their school or a school-zone warning — any safety-communicating sign is valid. Oral explanation accepted if writing is a barrier.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing allows students to express visual understanding of signage design; the sentence anchors it in meaning and demonstrates the communicative intent.

assessment_items.task: Write your own 'Safe Travel Rules' list with at least four rules. Include at least one rule for travelling in a vehicle and at least one rule for walking or cycling on a road. For each rule, write one reason why it keeps you or others safe.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: What should you do inside a bus or car? What should you do on the footpath? What should a cyclist do? Use the format: Rule: ___ / Reason: ___
format_of_output: A list of at least four rules
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any well-reasoned safety rule drawn from the student's own experience or the chapter discussion. Rules need not be identical to the textbook list — assess whether the rule names a specific safe behaviour and whether the reason connects it to the safety outcome (preventing injury, protecting others, following the law). Regional transport contexts (auto-rickshaw, bicycle, school van) are equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate and apply safety rules for different modes of travel and road use.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can name specific safe behaviours for different travel contexts and explain why each rule protects the traveller or others — moving beyond recall to purposeful reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The rule-reason format ensures students do not simply list words but attach meaning. A list of rules without reasons shows recall only; reasons show understanding.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific, actionable rules (e.g. 'Always walk on the footpath — cars cannot hit you there') with a clear safety reason. Weak: vague entries ('be careful') with no explanation of what the behaviour is or why it matters.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students from areas with different road conditions (unpaved roads, no footpaths) may write rules suited to their context — these are equally valid. Oral dictation to the teacher is accepted if writing is a barrier.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The rule-reason structure makes the safety reasoning explicit and observable, allowing the teacher to assess both knowledge and understanding of purpose.

assessment_items.question_text: Rishi saw many flowers in his cousin's garden. Some flowers — like rose and marigold — he already knew. Others — like tulip and buransh — were new to him. Name two flowers from the chapter that grow in specific mountain or regional areas of India. For each flower, write the region or state it is associated with.
expected_elements: Names two flowers from the chapter (from among: tulip, buransh/Rhododendron, amaltas, sakhua)
Correctly matches each flower to its associated region (tulip → Kashmir; buransh/Rhododendron → Jammu; amaltas → Kerala; sakhua → Jharkhand)
Response is presented clearly — either as two labelled pairs or two sentences
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit: two correct flower-region pairs. Partial credit: one correct pair. Accept 'Rhododendron' as an alternative name for buransh. Deduct if the student names only familiar flowers (rose, marigold, hibiscus) which the chapter presents as flowers Rishi already knew everywhere, not region-specific.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record diversity among plants by matching them to the regional environments in which they grow.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

expected_elements: Names two flowers from the chapter that are presented as region-specific (tulip, buransh/Rhododendron, amaltas, or sakhua)
Correctly pairs each flower to its region or state (tulip-Kashmir, buransh-Jammu, amaltas-Kerala, sakhua-Jharkhand)
Response is organised so both flowers and both regions are clearly identifiable

assessment_items.question_text: Mami explained to the children why people celebrate festivals in spring. She said that after winter, flowers bloom, grass grows, and new leaves appear. What does this tell us about the connection between spring festivals and nature?

options.label: A
options.text: Spring festivals are a way communities celebrate the renewal of nature after winter.

options.label: B
options.text: Spring festivals are celebrated because elders give sweets and blessings to children.

options.label: C
options.text: Spring festivals are celebrated because markets open and new goods arrive.

options.label: D
options.text: Spring festivals happen because it is warm enough to travel to other villages.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests whether students understand Mami's explanation — that spring festivals are a cultural response to the seasonal renewal of nature — which is the chapter's central linking idea between the natural and human-cultural strands.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a seasonal change in nature and the cultural practices communities develop in response to it.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has connected festivals to economic activity (markets, goods) rather than natural seasonal change — a plausible but chapter-unsupported idea that shows confusion with other cultural learning.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has noted travel as part of the chapter but misidentified it as the cause of the festival rather than a consequence of the community gathering that festivals create.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has recalled a specific detail from Rishi's spring ritual (elders giving sweets) and mistaken a practice within the festival for the reason the festival exists — showing surface recall without grasping the nature-culture link.

assessment_items.question_text: In the chapter, children are asked to find out from their elders which festivals are celebrated in their locality in different seasons, and what special foods are made. Choose one season and write: (a) the name of one festival celebrated in that season in your area, and (b) one special food made during that festival.
expected_elements: Names one season clearly (summer, monsoon/rainy, autumn/winter, or spring)
Names a festival associated with that season in the student's own locality or the chapter's examples
Names one special food prepared during that festival
assessment_items.annotation: Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct. Students may name festivals and foods from their own community that do not appear in the textbook — these should be accepted and affirmed. Assess whether the season, festival, and food are internally consistent (e.g. a winter festival with winter-appropriate food) rather than whether they match any single regional example. The textbook examples (Thekua-Chhath Puja, Pitha-Bihu, Gujiya-Holi, Sadya-Onam, etc.) are correct if students cite them.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple structured inquiry by drawing on elder knowledge to document seasonal festivals, foods, and clothing practices in their own community.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: A festival plausibly linked to that season in the student's own region or in the chapter's examples
A specific food (not just 'sweets' or 'food') associated with that festival

assessment_items.question_text: Festivals bring people together — relatives travel from far away, communities gather, and everyone shares food, music, and joy. Think about a festival you have celebrated with your family or community. Explain how that festival brought people together and made the community feel connected.
look_for: Names or describes a specific festival the student has personally experienced or knows about
Identifies at least one way people came together (relatives visiting, shared cooking, communal gathering, procession, singing or dancing)
Connects the coming-together to a sense of shared joy, belonging, or community bond
Uses at least one concrete detail (a food, a ritual, a relative, a place) to make the response specific rather than generic
assessment_items.annotation: Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct. Students may describe any festival from any community — the chapter deliberately presents diversity across four regions. Assess the quality of reasoning (how the described activity created connection) rather than the festival's name or origin. A response that names a festival but describes only individual experience without a community dimension is partial.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect personal experiences of family and community gatherings to the broader idea that festivals and celebrations build bonds across distances.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

look_for: A specific festival is identified (not just 'a festival in my town')
At least one community-gathering mechanism is described (relatives travelling, shared meal, procession, communal song or dance, shared decoration)
The student explains — not just states — how that mechanism created a feeling of togetherness or belonging
At least one concrete, specific detail grounds the response (a named food, a named relative, a ritual action, a place where people gathered)

assessment_items.task: Choose two spaces in your school. Design a signboard for each space. Your signboard should have: a symbol or picture that shows what the space is for, the name of the space written below the symbol, and one sentence explaining what the sign means for someone who has never been to your school.
assessment_items.scaffold: First, think: What does someone need to know about this space? Choose a clear symbol — a book for the library, a tap for drinking water, and so on. Draw your symbol inside a box or shape. Write the name of the space below. Then write: 'This sign tells you ___.'
format_of_output: Two signboard drawings, each with a symbol, a space name label, and one explanatory sentence
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two school spaces from the textbook list (library, toilet, assembly, drinking water point, playground, classroom, stairs) or other school spaces the student chooses. Assess whether the symbol clearly communicates the space's function, whether the label matches the symbol, and whether the explanatory sentence is consistent and informative for an unfamiliar visitor. Artistic quality is not assessed.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and explain visual signs that communicate purpose or direction clearly to a shared community of users.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the concept of visual communication — learned through road signs and school signboards — to create signs that serve a shared community of users with varied language backgrounds.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks students through three steps: choosing a symbol, labelling the space, and writing an explanatory sentence. A strong response completes all three for both signs; a partial response omits the sentence or the label.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a recognisable symbol clearly matched to the space, an accurate label, and a sentence that explains the sign's purpose to a newcomer. Weak: a decorative drawing without a label, or a label without a symbol, or a sentence that restates the label rather than explaining it.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe their symbol in words and draw a simple outline — the key assessment is whether they can explain the communicative function of the sign. Students may choose spaces not on the textbook list if they explain their choice.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing makes the visual communication strategy concrete; the sentence demonstrates that the student understands the sign's social purpose — guiding someone unfamiliar with the space.
